To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

InsP( 3)-induced oscillations in intralumenal Ca(2+), H(+), and pH can turn mast cell granule into Ca(2+)/ H(+) oscillators that release both Ca(2+) "and" H(+), and that the low pH in the granular compartment has important implications for intracellular processes.

InsP( 3 )-induced Ca( 2 + ) oscillations can trigger ATP-independent oscillations in the intraluminal pH of mast cell secretory vesicles, and that the perigranular H(+) and Ca(2+) released from the granules oscillate in phase with each other but out-of-phase to the corresponding intraluminal H(+) oscillations.
InsP( 3) turns secretory granules of mast cells into oscillating H(+) and Ca(2+) sources.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of InsP( 3)-receptor Ca(2+)-release channels as integrators of intracellular Ca(2+) information.
the development of novel tools for the analysis and quantification of the dynamic properties of secretory granules.
understanding how cells use the oscillating properties of secretory granules to encode and transmit intracellular information.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
InsP(4)-induced intracellular Ca(2+) or H(+) oscillators are ATP-independent and are the result of a coordinated action of Ca( 2+) and H(+) oscillating signals.
InsP( 3) can turn granules into Ca2+ oscillators, into proton oscillators, and into oscillators of Ca2+ release.
InsP( 3) is the link between the extracellular information network and the intracellular information system of the cell.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
InsP( 3 ) is not only an important link in intracellular information networks but also an important link in intercellular communication.
InsP(4)-induced Ca2+ and pH oscillations are the first examples of a new type of intracellular signal that could significantly increase the information capacity of the intracellular network.
InsP( 3)-receptor channel activation on the granular surface turns secretory organelles into oscillators of Ca(2+), H(+), and pH.
The main takeaway from our work is that

InsP( 3) is a powerful signal integrator that can turn secretory compartments into Ca(2+)/pH oscillators and that these Ca(2+)/ pH oscillators can encode a complex information network that could be critical for signal transduction.
granules might not only be the "storage" but also the "transduction" unit in secretory cells.
the secretory compartment can encode a combined Ca/H+ signal that can be decoded in a specific manner by proteins in its immediate vicinity.
